newsitem.title: USA: Texans return to polls for Congressional run-offs.
newsitem.headline: Texans return to polls for Congressional run-offs.

text.p: Texas voters returned to the polls Tuesday in special congressional run-off elections to fill the final three seats in the U.S. House.

Federal poll-watchers were monitoring voting in two counties where blacks were harassed in early voting that ended last week and allegations of voter fraud were lodged against the campaign of freshman Republican Representative Steve Stockman.
Voting was expected to be light as polls opened Tuesday, with 10 percent to 30 percent of eligible voters in the three Houston-area districts likely to turn out.
Voters in west Texas also were voting in a run-off election that could give Republicans majority control in the state Senate for the first time in 124 years.
Election day brought an end to negative political advertising by both parties in the past week as campaigns worked to energise voters into making a special trip to the polls.

"I think in general it may turn a few marginal voters away from the polls," University of Houston political scientist Robert Erikson said of mudslinging that characterised the House run-off campaigns.

Allegations of voter fraud surfaced in the 9th district, where supporters of Democratic challenger Nick Lampson claimed blacks were being harassed and likely Republican voters enticed to the polls with promises of free hams and turkeys by Stockman supporters.

The U.S. Justice Department sent 24 federal observers to monitor polling places and vote-counting in Galveston and Jefferson counties after uncovering evidence minority voters were harassed in early voting last week.

Stockman came under fire during the campaign for ties to rightwing militias following the bombing of the Oklahoma City federal building and aides said he was trailing in the early voting that ended Friday.

The run-off elections were called after no candidates won majorities in the districts, among 13 redrawn after a federal court panel ruled that two districts in Houston and one in Dallas had been racially gerrymandered.

Republicans are assured of holding onto their seat in the 8th district in Houston's northern suburbs, where two Republicans, state Representative Kevin Brady and physician Gene Fontenot, squared off for the fourth time this year.

Brady ran ahead of Fontenot in the March party primary and won the primary run-off, then topped Fontenot 41-39 percent in the Nov. 5 primary. Fontenot reentered the race after it was opened to all comers when the district was redrawn. The seat was vacated by the retirement of Representative Jack Fields, who served 16 years in the House.

In the 25th district in southeast Houston, Republican challenger Dolly Madison McKenna was facing strong opposition from the religious right, angered over her pro-choice stand on abortion. Anti-abortion groups were encouraging voters to file blank ballots to protest the abortion-rights positions of McKenna and incumbent Democratic Representative Ken Bentsen, nephew of former U.S. Sen. and Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen.

If Republicans manage to sweep the run-off elections, Democrats would lose control of the Texas congressional delegation for the first time. But the races will not tip the balance of power in Congress, where the Republicans held a 227-205 House majority following the November elections.
